atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Before we can ask *why* things move, we need a vocabulary for *how* they move. Picture filming a sprinter. At every instant the camera can tell you three things: where she is, how fast she is going, and whether she is speeding up. Kinematics is exactly this language of motion — pure description, no forces, no causes. It is the surveying that everything else in mechanics is built on top of.

### Precisely

Three quantities, each the time-rate of change of the one before it:

- **Position** $\vec{r}(t)$ — a vector pointing from a chosen origin to the object. Units: metres ($\text{m}$).
- **Velocity** $\vec{v} = \dfrac{d\vec{r}}{dt}$ — how position changes per unit time. Units: $\text{m/s}$.
- **Acceleration** $\vec{a} = \dfrac{d\vec{v}}{dt} = \dfrac{d^2\vec{r}}{dt^2}$ — how velocity changes per unit time. Units: $\text{m/s}^2$.

The arrows matter: these are **vectors**, carrying direction as well as size. When $\vec{a}$ is *constant*, integrating once and twice gives the standard kinematic equations:

$$\vec{v} = \vec{v}_0 + \vec{a}\,t, \qquad \vec{r} = \vec{r}_0 + \vec{v}_0 t + \tfrac{1}{2}\vec{a}\,t^2.$$

### Worked example

A car starts at rest ($v_0 = 0$) and accelerates at $a = 3\ \text{m/s}^2$ for $t = 5\ \text{s}$.

- Final speed: $v = v_0 + at = 0 + (3)(5) = 15\ \text{m/s}$.
- Distance covered: $x = v_0 t + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2 = 0 + \tfrac{1}{2}(3)(25) = 37.5\ \text{m}$.

Notice the distance grows with $t^2$ — doubling the time quadruples the distance, the signature of constant acceleration.

### Why it works

The relations are just the definition of a derivative read in reverse. Acceleration is the slope of the velocity-vs-time graph; if that slope is constant, velocity is a straight line, and the area under a straight line is a triangle plus a rectangle — precisely the $v_0 t + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$ terms. The **fundamental theorem of calculus** guarantees that accumulating (integrating) a rate gives back the total change.

### Where it connects

Kinematics is the input layer for **Newton's laws**, which supply the missing *cause* ($\vec{F} = m\vec{a}$). Treating velocity as a full vector is what makes circular and curved motion intelligible, and it feeds directly into **work–energy** and **momentum**.

### Watch out

The most common trap: confusing **speed** with **velocity**. Speed is just the magnitude $|\vec{v}|$; velocity includes direction. An object rounding a curve at a steady $30\ \text{km/h}$ has constant speed but *changing* velocity, so it is accelerating — its velocity vector is being rotated even though its length is fixed. Constant speed does **not** mean zero acceleration.


### A closer look at the three layers

It helps to see the three quantities as a chain of questions about a graph. Plot position against time: the **slope** of that curve at any instant is the velocity. Now plot velocity against time: the slope of *that* curve is the acceleration, and the **area** under it is the change in position. This dual relationship — slope going one way, area going the other — is the entire content of kinematics, and it is why a single graph can answer almost any motion question. In one dimension the signs carry meaning too: a negative velocity means moving backward, and an acceleration opposite to the velocity means slowing down (not necessarily "negative acceleration in space").

### One more worked case

Suppose a ball is thrown straight up at $v_0 = 20\ \text{m/s}$ with downward $a = -9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$. It reaches its peak when $v = 0$: from $v = v_0 + at$, $t = 20/9.8 \approx 2.04\ \text{s}$. Its peak height is $x = v_0 t + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2 = (20)(2.04) - \tfrac{1}{2}(9.8)(2.04)^2 \approx 20.4\ \text{m}$. Notice the velocity passes smoothly through zero while the acceleration never does — gravity keeps pulling even at the top, which is exactly why the ball does not hover.
atoms.title: Kinematics — describing motion
atoms.summary: Position, velocity, and acceleration are the three layers of motion, each the time-derivative of the one before.

depths.eli5: Imagine watching a toy car. Three simple questions describe its motion: Where is it right now? How fast is it going? And is its speed changing? 'Position' is just where something is. 'Velocity' is how fast it moves and in which direction. 'Acceleration' is how quickly that velocity is changing — speeding up, slowing down, or turning. Kinematics is the part of physics that only describes motion; it never yet asks why the car moves.
depths.core: Kinematics describes how things move without yet asking what causes the motion (that 'why' is dynamics, covered later). A 'rate of change' means how fast one quantity changes as another (here, time) changes — in calculus this is called a derivative. Velocity is the rate of change of position over time; acceleration is the rate of change of velocity over time. When acceleration is constant, these relations can be added up (integrated) into the familiar formulas v = v₀ + at (speed grows steadily) and x = x₀ + v₀t + ½at² (position).
depths.deep: Velocity and acceleration are vectors — quantities that carry both a size and a direction (see the Vectors atom). Because direction counts, an object moving in a circle at constant speed is still accelerating: its speed (magnitude) is unchanged but its direction is constantly turning, so the velocity vector changes. Motion along a curved path (curvilinear motion) is where treating these quantities as full vectors stops being optional.

atoms.note: Constant speed is not the same as constant velocity: 'speed' is just the number, 'velocity' includes direction, so turning at a steady speed is still acceleration.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Some quantities are just numbers — temperature, mass, time. Others refuse to be captured by a single number because they point somewhere: a wind of $20\ \text{km/h}$ *to the north-east*, a force *downward*. Those directional quantities are **vectors**, and almost everything in physics is one. To do physics we need two ways of "multiplying" arrows: one that measures how much they line up, and one that measures how much they twist around each other.

### Precisely

A vector has a magnitude and a direction; a plain number is a **scalar**. For two vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ separated by angle $\theta$:

- **Dot product** (gives a scalar): $\;\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = ab\cos\theta$, where $a=|\vec a|$, $b=|\vec b|$. It is largest when they are parallel, zero when perpendicular.
- **Cross product** (gives a vector): $\;|\vec{a}\times\vec{b}| = ab\sin\theta$, pointing perpendicular to *both* $\vec a$ and $\vec b$, with direction set by the right-hand rule. It is zero when they are parallel, largest when perpendicular.

In components, $\vec a\cdot\vec b = a_xb_x + a_yb_y + a_zb_z$.

### Worked example

Take $\vec a = (3,0,0)$ and $\vec b = (0,4,0)$ (perpendicular, lengths 3 and 4).

- Dot product: $\vec a\cdot\vec b = 3\cdot0 + 0\cdot4 + 0\cdot0 = 0$ — consistent with $\cos 90^\circ = 0$.
- Cross product magnitude: $|\vec a\times\vec b| = 3\cdot4\cdot\sin90^\circ = 12$, pointing along $+z$ (out of the page).

### Why it works

The dot product picks out the **component** of one vector along the other: $\vec a\cdot\hat b$ is the shadow $\vec a$ casts on $\vec b$. That is exactly the projection geometry needs. The cross product is antisymmetric, $\vec a\times\vec b = -\,\vec b\times\vec a$, which is why swapping order flips the resulting arrow — the origin of every right-hand rule in magnetism and rotation.

### Where it connects

Work is a dot product, $W = \vec F\cdot\vec d$ — only the part of the force along the motion counts. Torque is a cross product, $\vec\tau = \vec r\times\vec F$. The **Lorentz force** $q\vec v\times\vec B$ and **angular momentum** $\vec r\times\vec p$ are cross products too.

### Watch out

Do not mix up the two products. The dot product is a *number* and peaks for parallel vectors; the cross product is a *vector* and peaks for perpendicular ones. A frequent error is forgetting that the cross product is special to three dimensions and that its direction needs the right-hand rule — get the hand wrong and every sign in your magnetism problem flips.


### Components, the practical workhorse

In practice we rarely use angles directly; we break vectors into **components** along chosen axes. A vector $\vec a$ becomes $(a_x, a_y, a_z)$, and then $\vec a\cdot\vec b = a_xb_x + a_yb_y + a_zb_z$ — no angle needed. The cross product has the determinant form $\vec a\times\vec b = (a_yb_z - a_zb_y,\ a_zb_x - a_xb_z,\ a_xb_y - a_yb_x)$. These component formulas are what computers actually evaluate, and they make the geometric meanings ($\cos\theta$ for alignment, $\sin\theta$ for the perpendicular twist) computable from raw coordinates.

### Why the perpendicularity matters

The fact that $\vec a\times\vec b$ is perpendicular to its inputs is not a quirk — it is the reason rotation and magnetism live in three dimensions so naturally. A spinning wheel has an angular-velocity vector pointing along its axle, perpendicular to the plane of spin; a current-carrying wire feels a force perpendicular to both the current and the field. Whenever a phenomenon "turns a corner" out of a plane, a cross product is usually lurking underneath.
atoms.title: Vectors and the dot/cross product
atoms.summary: Physical quantities with direction are vectors; the dot product measures alignment and the cross product measures perpendicular twist.

depths.eli5: Think of an arrow drawn on paper: it has a length and it points somewhere. That is a 'vector' — a quantity with both a size and a direction. Plain numbers (like temperature) have no direction; vectors do. There are two ways to 'multiply' two arrows. The dot product is a single number that tells you how much the two arrows point the same way (biggest when they line up, zero when they're at a right angle). The cross product makes a brand-new arrow that sticks straight out sideways from both of them.
depths.core: Force, velocity, and field are vectors — quantities with direction — not just plain numbers (which physicists call scalars). The angle between two vectors is θ (the Greek letter 'theta'). The dot product a·b = ab cosθ measures how aligned they are and produces a scalar; for example, work equals force·displacement (only the part of the force along the motion counts). The cross product a×b produces a new vector perpendicular (at a right angle) to both, with size ab sinθ; for example, torque (twisting effort) equals r×F. Here cos and sin are the cosine and sine functions from trigonometry.
depths.deep: The cross product is special to three-dimensional space and is antisymmetric — swapping the order flips the sign (a×b = −b×a). This is why 'right-hand rules' (point your fingers one way, your thumb gives the result's direction) appear everywhere in magnetism and rotation. In higher dimensions the true generalization is the wedge product, or equivalently an antisymmetric tensor (a more general directional object).

quiz.answer: The dot product gives a scalar measuring alignment (ab cosθ); the cross product gives a perpendicular vector measuring the twist between them (ab sinθ).

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Nature rarely hands you the answer directly. Instead it tells you how things *change* from one instant to the next — and leaves you to add up those changes. Two operations do this. A **derivative** asks "how fast is this changing right now?" (a speedometer reading). An **integral** asks "if I add up all these tiny changes, what is the total?" (the trip odometer). The magic is that they are inverses of each other.

### Precisely

For a quantity $f(t)$:

- The **derivative** $\dfrac{df}{dt}$ is the instantaneous rate of change — the slope of the curve at a point.
- The **integral** $\displaystyle\int f\,dt$ accumulates $f$ over an interval — the area under the curve.

They are tied by the **fundamental theorem of calculus**:

$$\int_{t_1}^{t_2}\frac{df}{dt}\,dt = f(t_2) - f(t_1).$$

In words: integrating a rate of change over an interval returns the net change. Units follow the quantities — if $f$ is velocity ($\text{m/s}$) then $\int f\,dt$ is a displacement ($\text{m}$).

### Worked example

Let velocity be $v(t) = 6t$ (so acceleration is constant, $dv/dt = 6$). The distance travelled from $t=0$ to $t=2$ is

$$\int_0^2 6t\,dt = \left[3t^2\right]_0^2 = 3(4) - 0 = 12\ \text{m}.$$

Differentiating $x(t)=3t^2$ gives back $v=6t$ — the two operations undo each other.

### Why it works

A definite integral is the limit of summing thin rectangles of width $dt$ and height $f$. Each rectangle is an infinitesimal change; the fundamental theorem says these infinitesimal pieces telescope into the overall difference $f(t_2)-f(t_1)$. This is why every conservation law and equation of motion can be "solved" by integration.

### Where it connects

Physical laws are usually **differential equations** — rules phrased in derivatives. Newton's $\vec F = m\,d^2\vec r/dt^2$ is one. The spatial cousins — **gradient**, **divergence**, **curl** — are exactly the language of **Maxwell's equations**, and the **least-action** principle is an integral made stationary.

### Watch out

Beginners often treat integration as "antidifferentiation only" and forget the **constant of integration** (set by initial conditions like $v_0$ or $x_0$). Drop it and your predicted motion starts from the wrong place. Also: a derivative is *local* (one instant), an integral is *global* (a whole interval) — keep straight which one a problem is asking for.


### The grammar of physical law

Almost every fundamental law is stated as a relationship between a quantity and its rate of change, then solved by integration. Radioactive decay obeys $dN/dt = -\lambda N$ (the more atoms, the more decays), whose solution is the exponential $N = N_0 e^{-\lambda t}$. Newtonian motion obeys $m\,d^2x/dt^2 = F$. Heat flow, population growth, circuit currents — all are differential equations. Learning physics is, to a large degree, learning to read these "change-rules" and integrate them under the right initial conditions.

### A second worked case

Integrate a constant acceleration to *derive* the kinematic equations. Start from $dv/dt = a$. Integrating: $v(t) = v_0 + at$. Integrate again, since $dx/dt = v$: $x(t) = x_0 + v_0 t + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$. The two arbitrary constants $v_0$ and $x_0$ are the initial velocity and position — exactly the "constant of integration" made physical. This is the same machinery, applied twice, that underlies every projectile-motion problem.
atoms.title: Derivatives and integrals for physics
atoms.summary: Differentiation extracts rates of change and integration accumulates them; physics is written almost entirely in this language.

depths.eli5: Two ideas power almost all of physics. A 'derivative' answers: how fast is something changing at this exact instant? (Like a car's speedometer reading right now.) An 'integral' does the opposite: it adds up countless tiny pieces to get a total. (Like adding up every tiny bit of distance to get the whole trip.) The neat part: they undo each other, the way adding and subtracting do.
depths.core: A 'differential equation' is a rule written in terms of how fast things change (their rates) rather than the answer directly. Nearly every physical law is a differential equation, and solving it means integrating — adding up the rates to find the actual quantity. The fundamental theorem of calculus is the bridge: if you integrate the derivative (rate of change) of something across an interval, you get back the net change of that something over the interval.
depths.deep: Vector calculus extends these ideas to fields — quantities defined at every point in space (like temperature in a room, or the electric field). The spatial derivatives are the gradient (which way a quantity increases fastest), divergence (how much a field spreads out from a point), and curl (how much it swirls around a point). Stokes' theorem and the divergence theorem are the multidimensional versions of the fundamental theorem, and they are exactly the machinery Maxwell's equations of electromagnetism are written in.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Why do things move the way they do? For two thousand years people thought motion needed continuous pushing. Newton's insight was the opposite: *coasting is the natural state*, and a force is needed only to *change* motion. Three short laws then turn any list of forces into a complete prediction of the future.

### Precisely

- **First law (inertia):** with zero net force, velocity stays constant. This defines an **inertial frame** — a viewpoint not itself accelerating.
- **Second law:** the net force equals the rate of change of momentum,
$$\vec F = \frac{d\vec p}{dt}, \qquad \vec p = m\vec v.$$
For constant mass this is the famous $\vec F = m\vec a$. Units: force in newtons ($1\ \text{N} = 1\ \text{kg·m/s}^2$).
- **Third law:** forces come in equal-and-opposite pairs, $\vec F_{12} = -\vec F_{21}$, acting on *two different bodies*.

### Worked example

A $2\ \text{kg}$ block is pushed with a net force of $10\ \text{N}$.

$$a = \frac{F}{m} = \frac{10\ \text{N}}{2\ \text{kg}} = 5\ \text{m/s}^2.$$

If instead two forces act, $8\ \text{N}$ right and $3\ \text{N}$ left, the *net* force is $5\ \text{N}$ right, giving $a = 2.5\ \text{m/s}^2$. Only the vector sum matters.

### Why it works

The second law is the engine. Combined with the third law it guarantees **momentum conservation**: for two interacting bodies, $d\vec p_1/dt + d\vec p_2/dt = \vec F_{21} + \vec F_{12} = 0$, so the total is constant. By Noether's theorem this conservation is the shadow of the *homogeneity of space* — physics is the same here as there.

### Where it connects

Newton's laws sit on top of **kinematics** and **vectors** and feed directly into **momentum**, **work–energy**, **rotational motion**, and **gravitation**. The momentum form $\vec F = d\vec p/dt$ survives intact into **special relativity**, even though $\vec p$ is no longer simply $m\vec v$.

### Watch out

The classic blunder with the third law: thinking the action–reaction pair *cancels*. It cannot — the two forces act on **different objects**. When you push a wall, your push acts on the wall and the wall's push acts on you. A rocket flies because it pushes exhaust backward and the exhaust pushes the rocket forward — different bodies, no cancellation.


### Free-body diagrams: how the laws are used

In practice you apply the second law by drawing a **free-body diagram** — a sketch of a single object with every force on it drawn as an arrow — then summing those arrows component by component and setting the total equal to $m\vec a$. The art is including all real forces (gravity, normal, tension, friction, applied) and *only* forces that act *on that object*. The third law then reminds you that any force the object exerts back appears on a *different* free-body diagram, never its own.

### Inertial frames and why they matter

The first law quietly defines the stage on which the others play: an **inertial frame**, one not itself accelerating. In a braking car you feel thrown forward not because a force pushes you but because the car (your frame) decelerates while your body tries to continue — the first law in action. In a genuinely accelerating frame, "fictitious" forces (centrifugal, Coriolis) appear as bookkeeping corrections. Newton's laws in their clean form hold only in inertial frames, which is why identifying the frame is the first step of any problem.
atoms.title: Newton's three laws of motion
atoms.summary: Inertia, F = ma, and action–reaction together turn forces into predicted motion.

depths.eli5: Three simple rules explain almost all everyday motion. (1) Things keep doing what they're doing — sitting still or coasting in a straight line — unless something pushes or pulls them. That tendency is called inertia. (2) A push changes an object's motion: a stronger push changes it more, and a heavier object changes less. (3) Every push comes with an equal push back the other way — when you push on a wall, the wall pushes on you.
depths.core: A 'force' is a push or pull; the 'net force' is the total once all pushes and pulls are added as vectors. First law: with no net force, velocity stays constant (this property is inertia, and frames of reference where it holds are called inertial frames). Second law: net force equals the rate of change of momentum, F = dp/dt, where momentum p = mv (mass times velocity); for constant mass this simplifies to the famous F = ma (force = mass × acceleration). Third law: forces always come in equal-and-opposite pairs acting on two different bodies. Once you know the forces, these laws make the future motion fully predictable (deterministic).
depths.deep: The deep content is the second law's identification of force with dp/dt (the rate of change of momentum), which survives into Einstein's relativity even though momentum p there is no longer simply mv. The third law guarantees conservation of momentum for isolated systems — and, via Noether's theorem, that conservation is secretly a statement about the uniformity (homogeneity) of space: physics works the same here as over there.

atoms.note: Action and reaction act on different bodies, so they never cancel on the same object.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

In a chaotic collision — billiard balls scattering, cars crumpling — tracking the exact forces during impact is hopeless. Yet there is one quantity that behaves with perfect discipline: the total **momentum**. Whatever the mess in between, the grand total of "mass times velocity" is identical before and after. It is the cleanest bookkeeping tool in mechanics.

### Precisely

Momentum of one object is $\vec p = m\vec v$ (units $\text{kg·m/s}$). For a system with no external force — an **isolated system** — the total is conserved:

$$\sum_i \vec p_{i,\text{before}} = \sum_i \vec p_{i,\text{after}}.$$

This is a vector equation: it holds separately for each direction.

### Worked example

A $2\ \text{kg}$ cart moving at $3\ \text{m/s}$ strikes a stationary $1\ \text{kg}$ cart and they stick together. Find the final speed $v$.

$$\underbrace{(2)(3) + (1)(0)}_{\text{before}} = \underbrace{(2+1)\,v}_{\text{after}} \;\Rightarrow\; 6 = 3v \;\Rightarrow\; v = 2\ \text{m/s}.$$

We solved it without knowing a single thing about the messy contact force — only the before and after states.

### Why it works

It follows directly from Newton. Each internal force is half of a third-law pair, $\vec F_{12} = -\vec F_{21}$, so when you add up $d\vec p_i/dt$ over the whole system the internal forces cancel exactly. Only *external* forces can change the total. By Noether's theorem, this conservation is the dynamical face of **translational symmetry** — the laws don't care where you are.

### Where it connects

Momentum conservation is the parent of **rotational** angular-momentum conservation and the thermodynamic pressure of **kinetic theory**. It persists in relativity with $\vec p = \gamma m\vec v$ and in quantum mechanics.

### Watch out

The condition is **zero net external force**, not "no forces at all." Internal forces between the colliding objects are fine — they always cancel. Also, energy and momentum are different ledgers: in an inelastic collision (carts sticking) momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is *not* — some becomes heat and deformation. Don't assume both are conserved.


### Impulse: the time-integrated force

There is a second, equally useful face of the second law. Integrating $\vec F = d\vec p/dt$ over time gives the **impulse**: $\int \vec F\,dt = \Delta\vec p$. This is why airbags and crumple zones save lives — they lengthen the collision time $\Delta t$, so the same momentum change is delivered by a much smaller average force. The change in momentum is fixed by the before-and-after velocities; only the *peak force* is negotiable, and stretching the time stretches the force down.

### Elastic versus inelastic

Collisions split into two types by what happens to kinetic energy. In an **elastic** collision (idealized billiard balls), both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved. In an **inelastic** one (the carts that stick), momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not — some becomes heat, sound, and deformation. The fully inelastic case, where objects move together afterward, is the easiest to solve and the one where the most kinetic energy is lost. Momentum, crucially, is conserved in *both* — that is what makes it the more reliable bookkeeping tool than energy.
atoms.title: Momentum and its conservation
atoms.summary: Total momentum of an isolated system is conserved — the cleanest bookkeeping tool for collisions.

depths.eli5: Momentum is a measure of 'how much motion' something has — mass times velocity (a heavy, fast thing has a lot). The big rule: in any crash where nothing outside is pushing on the group, the total momentum of everything involved is exactly the same right before and right after. It just gets shared around.
depths.core: An 'isolated system' is a group of objects with no outside (external) force acting on it. Because the objects' internal forces on each other cancel in Newton's third-law pairs (equal and opposite), the total momentum of an isolated system cannot change — it is 'conserved.' This is enormously useful: collisions become solvable even when the messy details of the forces during impact are unknown, because you only need the before and after states.
depths.deep: Conservation of momentum is the dynamical shadow of translational symmetry of space — the fact that physics is the same wherever you are — via Noether's theorem (every continuous symmetry has a matching conservation law). It also holds in relativity and quantum mechanics, with the relativistic momentum p = γmv (γ, 'gamma', is a speed-dependent stretch factor) replacing the simple mv.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Push a stalled car and it speeds up; the harder you push and the farther it rolls while you push, the faster it ends up going. That product — force acting over a distance — is **work**, and it is precisely the energy you pour into the car's motion. The work–energy theorem makes this exact: work in equals kinetic energy gained.

### Precisely

Work done by a force along a path is the line integral

$$W = \int \vec F\cdot d\vec r,$$

(units: joules, $1\ \text{J} = 1\ \text{N·m}$). Only the component of $\vec F$ along the motion contributes, because of the dot product. **Kinetic energy** is $K = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$. The **work–energy theorem** states:

$$W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K = \tfrac{1}{2}mv_f^2 - \tfrac{1}{2}mv_i^2.$$

### Worked example

A constant $20\ \text{N}$ force pushes a $4\ \text{kg}$ box (initially at rest) over $5\ \text{m}$ along the force's direction.

$$W = Fd = (20)(5) = 100\ \text{J}.$$

Then $W = \tfrac{1}{2}mv_f^2$, so $100 = \tfrac{1}{2}(4)v_f^2 = 2v_f^2$, giving $v_f = \sqrt{50} \approx 7.1\ \text{m/s}$.

### Why it works

Start from $\vec F = m\,d\vec v/dt$ and integrate along the path. Using $\vec v\,dt = d\vec r$,

$$\int \vec F\cdot d\vec r = m\int \frac{d\vec v}{dt}\cdot\vec v\,dt = m\int \vec v\cdot d\vec v = \Delta\!\left(\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2\right).$$

So the theorem is just Newton's second law integrated over distance rather than time.

### Where it connects

It is the gateway to **conservation of energy**: a conservative force lets you define a potential energy whose change equals the negative work. It also explains why a perpendicular force (magnetic, or the tension in **circular motion**) does no work at all.

### Watch out

A force perpendicular to the motion does **zero** work, even though it is a real force changing the velocity's direction. The string tension in uniform circular motion and the magnetic Lorentz force are the classic cases: they bend the path but never change the speed, so $\Delta K = 0$.


### Power: the rate of doing work

Closely tied to work is **power**, the rate at which work is done: $P = dW/dt = \vec F\cdot\vec v$ (units: watts, $1\ \text{W} = 1\ \text{J/s}$). A car engine rated at $100\ \text{kW}$ can deliver that much energy to the wheels each second; at high speed the same power produces less force, which is why acceleration tapers off. Power, not work, is what is usually limited by an engine or a person.

### Why energy methods are powerful

The deep convenience of the work–energy theorem is that it is a *scalar* statement — no directions to track, just an accounting of energy in and out. For a roller coaster, computing the speed at the bottom of a drop via forces would mean integrating a continuously changing normal force along a curve; via energy it is one line, $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = mgh$. Whenever you care about *speeds and heights* but not the detailed path, energy methods win. The price is that they tell you the speed but not the direction of motion, which forces sometimes must supply.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Energy is the universal currency of physics. It changes costume — motion (kinetic) into height or stretch (potential) and back — but for the right kind of force the total never changes. A pendulum trades speed for height endlessly; a ball rolls "downhill" toward lower stored energy. Conservation of energy is the accountant that always balances the books.

### Precisely

A **conservative force** is one whose work depends only on the endpoints, not the path. For such forces you can define a **potential energy** $U$ with

$$\vec F = -\nabla U,$$

where $\nabla U$ (the gradient) points in the direction $U$ increases fastest, so the minus sign makes the force point "downhill." The total **mechanical energy** is then conserved:

$$E = K + U = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + U = \text{const}.$$

### Worked example

A ball of mass $m = 2\ \text{kg}$ is dropped from height $h = 5\ \text{m}$ (take $g = 9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$, $U = mgh$). Find its speed at the ground.

Energy at top $= mgh = (2)(9.8)(5) = 98\ \text{J}$, all potential. At the ground it is all kinetic:

$$\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = 98 \;\Rightarrow\; v = \sqrt{\frac{2(98)}{2}} = \sqrt{98} \approx 9.9\ \text{m/s}.$$

### Why it works

For a conservative force the work–energy theorem gives $\Delta K = W = -\Delta U$, so $\Delta(K+U) = 0$. By Noether's theorem this is the shadow of **time-translation symmetry** — physics today equals physics tomorrow. A force admits a potential exactly when its curl vanishes (no built-in swirl).

### Where it connects

It builds directly on **work–energy** and underlies **simple harmonic motion**, **gravitation** (with $U = -GMm/r$), and the **first law of thermodynamics**, which extends the ledger to include heat.

### Watch out

Friction and drag are **non-conservative** — their work depends on the path, so mechanical energy is *not* conserved when they act. The energy isn't destroyed; it becomes heat. The total energy (now including thermal) is still conserved, but $K + U$ alone is not. Remember the minus sign in $\vec F = -\nabla U$: the force points toward *lower* potential.


### Reading a potential-energy curve

A graph of $U$ versus position is a complete map of one-dimensional motion. The force at any point is minus the slope, $F = -dU/dx$, so the object is pushed toward valleys. A **minimum** of $U$ is a stable equilibrium (a marble settles there); a **maximum** is unstable (a marble balanced on a hilltop). The total energy $E$ drawn as a horizontal line shows the "turning points" where $E = U$ and the object momentarily stops, and the region $E > U$ where motion is allowed. This single picture explains oscillation, escape, and binding all at once.

### Escape and binding

For gravity, $U = -GMm/r$, the curve rises toward zero at infinity. An object with total energy $E < 0$ is **bound** — it cannot reach infinity and orbits. With $E \ge 0$ it escapes. Setting $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 - GMm/r = 0$ gives the **escape velocity** $v = \sqrt{2GM/r}$, about $11.2\ \text{km/s}$ from Earth's surface — a direct, elegant payoff of energy conservation.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Spinning has its own complete set of rules that mirror straight-line motion. Instead of a push you apply a **twist** (a wrench on a bolt). Instead of plain mass, what matters is how far the mass sits from the axis. And just as a coasting object keeps coasting, a spinning object keeps its spin unless something twists it — which is why a figure skater speeds up by pulling her arms in.

### Precisely

Each linear quantity has a rotational partner:

- **Torque** $\vec\tau = \vec r\times\vec F$ (the analog of force; units $\text{N·m}$).
- **Moment of inertia** $I = \sum m_i r_i^2$ (the analog of mass — mass weighted by distance² from the axis).
- **Angular velocity** $\vec\omega$ (spin rate; $\text{rad/s}$) and **angular momentum** $\vec L = I\vec\omega$.

The rotational Newton's law is $\vec\tau = \dfrac{d\vec L}{dt}$. With no external torque, $\vec L$ is conserved.

### Worked example

A skater spins at $\omega_i = 2\ \text{rad/s}$ with $I_i = 6\ \text{kg·m}^2$. She pulls in her arms, lowering her moment of inertia to $I_f = 2\ \text{kg·m}^2$. With no external torque, $L = I\omega$ is conserved:

$$I_i\omega_i = I_f\omega_f \;\Rightarrow\; (6)(2) = (2)\,\omega_f \;\Rightarrow\; \omega_f = 6\ \text{rad/s}.$$

She triples her spin rate just by redistributing her mass.

### Why it works

Torque is what Newton's second law becomes when you take the cross product with $\vec r$: $\vec r\times\vec F = \vec r\times d\vec p/dt = d(\vec r\times\vec p)/dt = d\vec L/dt$. Angular momentum conservation reflects the **rotational symmetry** of space via Noether's theorem.

### Where it connects

It is the rotational sibling of **momentum** and **Newton's laws**, uses the **cross product** from vectors, and reappears quantized in **quantum spin** and the **hydrogen atom**.

### Watch out

The moment of inertia depends on *which axis* you choose and how the mass is spread — there is no single "$I$" for an object. And for a non-symmetric rigid body, $\vec L$ and $\vec\omega$ need not even point the same way ($I$ is really a matrix), which makes the free tumbling of irregular objects surprisingly complex.


### Where the moment of inertia comes from

For a continuous body, $I = \int r^2\,dm$ — every scrap of mass weighted by the square of its distance from the axis. This is why a hollow hoop ($I = mR^2$) is harder to spin than a solid disk of the same mass and radius ($I = \tfrac{1}{2}mR^2$): the hoop's mass all sits far from the axis. It is also why long objects are easier to rotate about their long axis than across it. The "square of the distance" is the reason small changes in how mass is arranged produce large changes in rotational inertia.

### Rolling: translation and rotation together

A wheel rolling without slipping couples the two motions: its center moves at $v = \omega R$, and its total kinetic energy is the sum $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + \tfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2$. This is why a solid cylinder beats a hoop down a ramp — the hoop stores more of its energy in rotation and less in forward speed. Rolling problems are a clean showcase of linear and rotational mechanics working in tandem, each with its own conserved quantities.

Angular momentum L = Iω (where ω, 'omega', is the spin rate) is the analog of momentum; it changes only when an external torque acts, so it is conserved for isolated systems. That is why a figure skater spins faster when pulling their arms in.
depths.deep: Angular momentum conservation reflects the rotational symmetry of space (physics looks the same in every direction) via Noether's theorem. Because the moment of inertia I depends on both the chosen axis and how the mass is distributed, rigid-body rotation is really a tensor relationship (L = Iω with I a matrix, not a single number), and the free rotation of an irregular object can be surprisingly complex.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Drop an apple and it falls; the Moon circles the Earth. Newton's leap was that these are the *same* phenomenon — every chunk of matter pulls on every other chunk. The pull weakens fast with distance: move twice as far away and it drops to a quarter. One simple law governs both the orchard and the heavens.

### Precisely

The force between two point masses $m_1$ and $m_2$ separated by distance $r$ is attractive, directed along the line joining them:

$$\vec F = -\frac{G m_1 m_2}{r^2}\,\hat r,$$

where $G = 6.674\times10^{-11}\ \text{N·m}^2/\text{kg}^2$ is the gravitational constant and $\hat r$ points from one mass to the other. Because it falls as $1/r^2$, this is an **inverse-square law**. The matching potential energy is $U = -\dfrac{Gm_1m_2}{r}$.

### Worked example

The gravitational force between the Earth ($m_1 = 5.97\times10^{24}\ \text{kg}$) and a $70\ \text{kg}$ person at the surface ($r = 6.37\times10^6\ \text{m}$):

$$F = \frac{(6.674\times10^{-11})(5.97\times10^{24})(70)}{(6.37\times10^6)^2} \approx 687\ \text{N}.$$

Dividing by the mass gives $g = F/m \approx 9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$ — the familiar surface gravity, derived from the universal law.

### Why it works

Combined with $\vec F = m\vec a$, the inverse-square law reproduces **Kepler's three laws** of planetary orbits — elliptical paths, equal areas in equal times, and $T^2 \propto a^3$. The Moon "falls" exactly like the apple, but its sideways velocity keeps it perpetually missing the Earth.

### Where it connects

It is the template for **Coulomb's law** (same $1/r^2$ form), obeys a **Gauss law**, and its puzzle — that gravitational and inertial mass are identical — seeds the **equivalence principle** and **general relativity**.

### Watch out

The $1/r^2$ refers to the distance between **centres** (for spherical bodies), not the distance to the surface. And note the sign convention: $U = -GMm/r$ is *negative* and approaches zero at infinity — a bound orbit has negative total energy. Forgetting the minus sign breaks every orbital-energy calculation.


### Orbits as a balance

A circular orbit is just gravity supplying exactly the centripetal force: $\dfrac{GMm}{r^2} = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$. Cancel $m$ and solve: $v = \sqrt{GM/r}$ — orbital speed depends only on the central mass and the radius, not on the orbiting object's mass. This is why a feather and a satellite at the same altitude orbit at the same speed. Rearranging gives Kepler's third law, $T^2 = \dfrac{4\pi^2}{GM}r^3$, tying period to radius for every planet around the Sun.

### The shell theorem

A beautiful consequence of the inverse-square law: a uniform spherical shell pulls on an outside object as if all its mass were at the center, and exerts *zero* net force on anything inside it. This is why we can treat the Earth as a point mass at its center for surface gravity, and why gravity actually *decreases* as you tunnel toward the center (the shell of matter above you stops contributing). The result holds only for the exact $1/r^2$ form — another sign of how special that geometry is.

Because the force shrinks with the square of distance, it is called an 'inverse-square law.' This single law explains both falling apples and the orbits of planets, and combined with F = ma it reproduces Kepler's laws of planetary motion. The matching potential energy is U = −Gm₁m₂/r.

Newton noticed they are exactly equal but had no explanation. Einstein later elevated this coincidence to the equivalence principle — the seed that grew into general relativity, his theory of gravity as curved spacetime.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Newton's method means drawing every push and pull as an arrow and breaking it into $x$, $y$, $z$ components — tedious, and awful when a bead is constrained to a curved wire. There is a slicker route. Write down a single scalar — kinetic energy minus potential energy — and one master equation grinds out the motion in *whatever* variables are most natural: an angle, a distance along a track, anything.

### Precisely

The **Lagrangian** is

$$L = T - V,$$

with $T$ the kinetic energy and $V$ the potential energy, written in **generalized coordinates** $q$ (any convenient variables) and their time-derivatives $\dot q$. The motion satisfies the **Euler–Lagrange equation**:

$$\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot q} - \frac{\partial L}{\partial q} = 0.$$

One such equation exists for each coordinate $q$.

### Worked example

A mass on a spring: $T = \tfrac{1}{2}m\dot x^2$, $V = \tfrac{1}{2}kx^2$, so $L = \tfrac{1}{2}m\dot x^2 - \tfrac{1}{2}kx^2$.

- $\dfrac{\partial L}{\partial \dot x} = m\dot x \Rightarrow \dfrac{d}{dt}(m\dot x) = m\ddot x.$
- $\dfrac{\partial L}{\partial x} = -kx.$

Euler–Lagrange: $m\ddot x - (-kx) = 0$, i.e. $m\ddot x = -kx$ — exactly Newton's spring equation, recovered with no force diagram.

### Why it works

The Euler–Lagrange equation is the condition that the **action** $S=\int L\,dt$ is stationary (the next atom). Because $L$ is a scalar, it is coordinate-free — constraints like "bead on a wire" are handled just by choosing the right $q$, with no constraint forces to compute.

### Where it connects

It is built on **energy conservation** and **calculus**, leads straight to the **principle of least action** and **Hamiltonian mechanics**, and is the natural home of **Noether's theorem** linking symmetry to conservation.

### Watch out

$L = T - V$ is a *difference*, not the total energy $T+V$ — a very common slip. Also, a coordinate missing from $L$ (a "cyclic" coordinate) means its conjugate momentum $\partial L/\partial\dot q$ is conserved; spotting these shortcuts is half the power of the method, so don't overlook which variables are absent.


### A genuinely awkward problem made easy

Consider a pendulum: a bob swinging on a rod of length $\ell$. In Newtonian terms you must resolve gravity and the rod's tension into components along a moving arc — fiddly. In Lagrangian terms, pick the angle $\theta$ as the coordinate. Then $T = \tfrac{1}{2}m\ell^2\dot\theta^2$ and $V = -mg\ell\cos\theta$, so $L = \tfrac{1}{2}m\ell^2\dot\theta^2 + mg\ell\cos\theta$. The Euler–Lagrange equation gives $m\ell^2\ddot\theta = -mg\ell\sin\theta$, i.e. $\ddot\theta = -(g/\ell)\sin\theta$ — the pendulum equation, with the constraint force (tension) never appearing.

### Why physicists prefer it

Beyond convenience, the Lagrangian framework generalizes. The *same* recipe — write down a Lagrangian, demand stationary action — extends to fields, relativity, and the Standard Model, where "forces" become terms in $L$ dictated by symmetry. Newton's vector forces are a special case; the scalar $L = T - V$ is the more portable idea, which is why nearly all of theoretical physics is phrased this way.

The Lagrangian is their difference, L = T − V, expressed using 'generalized coordinates' q — any convenient set of variables describing the configuration (an angle, a length, etc.) — and their rates of change (q̇, 'q-dot'). Plugging L into the Euler–Lagrange equation produces the equations of motion in any coordinate system, automatically respecting constraints (like a bead stuck on a wire) and never requiring you to break forces into x/y/z components. It gives the same physics as Newton's laws but is far more flexible.

This is Noether's theorem in action: a symmetry (the Lagrangian not caring about that coordinate) produces a conservation law. Lagrangian mechanics is the framework where symmetry and conservation become two faces of one structure.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Of all the conceivable routes an object could take from a fixed start to a fixed end, which one does nature actually choose? Astonishingly, there is a single criterion: a running total called the **action** sits at a tipping point along the true path — nudge the path a little and the action barely changes. From this one demand, all of classical mechanics falls out.

### Precisely

The **action** is the time-integral of the Lagrangian between fixed endpoints:

$$S = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} L\,dt.$$

The real trajectory makes $S$ **stationary** — a small variation $\delta$ of the path (with endpoints held fixed) produces no first-order change:

$$\delta S = 0.$$

Imposing this condition yields exactly the Euler–Lagrange equations.

### Worked example (conceptual)

Consider a free particle (no potential), $L = \tfrac{1}{2}m\dot x^2$. Among all paths from $x_1$ at $t_1$ to $x_2$ at $t_2$, the action is minimized by **constant velocity** — a straight line in space-time. Any wiggle adds extra $\dot x^2$ somewhere that must be paid back elsewhere, and squaring makes the average cost rise. So "least action" reproduces Newton's first law: a free particle moves in a straight line at constant speed.

### Why it works

Requiring $\delta S = 0$ is the **calculus of variations**: setting the first-order change to zero, integrating by parts, and using fixed endpoints leaves precisely $\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q} - \frac{\partial L}{\partial q} = 0$ at every instant. So the global principle and the local equation of motion are the same statement.

### Where it connects

It generalizes far beyond mechanics: field theory, **general relativity** (extremal proper time gives geodesics), optics (**Fermat's least time**), and — through Feynman's path integral — **quantum mechanics** are all action principles.

### Watch out

"Least" is a misnomer. The action is **stationary**, which may be a minimum *or* a saddle point, not always a true minimum. The condition is $\delta S = 0$ (a critical point), period — the path need not be the absolute shortest in action.


### The calculus of variations in one line

The mathematical engine is the **calculus of variations**, which finds the function (not just the number) that extremizes an integral. You imagine deforming the path by a tiny amount $\delta x(t)$ that vanishes at the endpoints, compute the first-order change in $S$, integrate by parts, and demand it vanish for *every* allowed deformation. The only way that can happen is if the integrand satisfies the Euler–Lagrange equation at each instant — so the global "best path" requirement collapses into a local equation of motion.

### A unifying thread across physics

What makes least action so celebrated is its reach. Light obeys it as **Fermat's principle** (least time). A particle in general relativity follows the path of extremal proper time. Most strikingly, Feynman showed quantum particles "try every path," each weighted by a phase $e^{iS/\hbar}$; the classical path is the one where neighboring paths' phases reinforce instead of cancel, because $S$ is stationary there. So the classical least-action principle is the $\hbar \to 0$ shadow of a quantum sum over all histories — arguably the deepest organizing idea in physics.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Here is yet another way to do mechanics, and the one that quantum theory grew out of. Instead of tracking position and velocity, you track position and **momentum**. A single energy function then tells you how both tick forward — not in one second-order equation, but in two clean, symmetric first-order ones.

### Precisely

The **Hamiltonian** $H(q,p)$ is obtained from the Lagrangian by a Legendre transform and usually equals the total energy $T+V$. The dynamics are **Hamilton's equations**:

$$\dot q = \frac{\partial H}{\partial p}, \qquad \dot p = -\frac{\partial H}{\partial q}.$$

The pair $(q,p)$ lives in **phase space**, whose axes are position and momentum. Note the symmetry — and the crucial minus sign in the second equation.

### Worked example

For a mass on a spring, $H = \dfrac{p^2}{2m} + \tfrac{1}{2}kx^2$.

- $\dot x = \dfrac{\partial H}{\partial p} = \dfrac{p}{m}$ (which says $p = m\dot x$, ordinary momentum).
- $\dot p = -\dfrac{\partial H}{\partial x} = -kx.$

Combine: $m\ddot x = \dot p = -kx$ — once again the spring equation, now from two first-order equations whose phase-space trajectory is an ellipse.

### Why it works

The Legendre transform swaps the velocity $\dot q$ for the momentum $p = \partial L/\partial\dot q$ as the independent variable. Splitting one second-order equation into two first-order ones reveals the symplectic geometry of phase space. **Liouville's theorem** then says a blob of nearby states keeps constant volume as it flows — a cornerstone of statistical mechanics.

### Where it connects

It builds on **Lagrangian mechanics**, anchors **statistical mechanics**, and is the launchpad for **quantum mechanics**: the Poisson bracket $\{q,p\}=1$ becomes the commutator $[\hat x,\hat p]=i\hbar$, and $H$ becomes the operator $\hat H$ in the **Schrödinger equation**.

### Watch out

Don't forget the minus sign in $\dot p = -\partial H/\partial q$ — its absence breaks energy conservation and the whole symplectic structure. Also, $H$ equals the total energy only under common conditions (time-independent, "natural" coordinates); in exotic cases $H$ and energy can differ.


### Phase space and the picture of motion

The real payoff of the Hamiltonian view is **phase space**, the plane (or higher space) with position on one axis and momentum on the other. A system's entire history becomes a single curve there. For an undamped oscillator the curve is a closed **ellipse** traced forever; add friction and it spirals inward to the origin. This geometric picture turns "solving the motion" into "drawing the flow," and it is the natural language of chaos theory, where nearby phase-space trajectories can diverge exponentially.

### The bridge to quantum mechanics

Hamiltonian mechanics is the scaffold quantum theory was built on. The classical **Poisson bracket** $\{q, p\} = 1$ — a rule encoding how position and momentum interrelate under the flow — is promoted, in quantization, to the commutator $[\hat x, \hat p] = i\hbar$. The Hamiltonian $H$ becomes the operator $\hat H$ that drives the Schrödinger equation. Almost every structural feature of quantum mechanics has a Hamiltonian-mechanics ancestor, which is why this reformulation, though it gives identical classical predictions, is the one physicists reach for at the frontier.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Pull a spring and release it: it oscillates back and forth at its own steady rhythm. The surprising fact is that the rhythm — how many wobbles per second — is the *same* whether you pulled it a little or a lot. Pendulums, guitar strings, and vibrating molecules all share this behavior. It is the single most reused pattern in physics.

### Precisely

When the restoring force is proportional to displacement, $F = -kx$ (Hooke's law, $k$ the stiffness), Newton's law $m\ddot x = -kx$ becomes

$$\ddot x = -\omega^2 x, \qquad \omega = \sqrt{k/m},$$

whose solution is sinusoidal, $x(t) = A\cos(\omega t + \phi)$. Here $\omega$ is the **angular frequency** ($\text{rad/s}$), $A$ the amplitude, and the period is $T = 2\pi/\omega$. Crucially, $\omega$ is **independent of amplitude**.

### Worked example

A $0.5\ \text{kg}$ mass on a spring of stiffness $k = 200\ \text{N/m}$:

$$\omega = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}} = \sqrt{\frac{200}{0.5}} = \sqrt{400} = 20\ \text{rad/s}, \qquad T = \frac{2\pi}{20} \approx 0.31\ \text{s}.$$

Pull it $2\ \text{cm}$ or $5\ \text{cm}$ — the period is still $0.31\ \text{s}$.

### Why it works

The defining equation $\ddot x = -\omega^2 x$ asks for a function whose second derivative is itself times a negative constant — exactly sine and cosine. Energy sloshes between kinetic $\tfrac{1}{2}m\dot x^2$ and potential $\tfrac{1}{2}kx^2$, their sum fixed. Amplitude-independence is what "linear restoring force" buys you.

### Why SHM is everywhere

Near the bottom of *any* smooth potential well, a Taylor expansion makes the potential look like a parabola, $U \approx \tfrac{1}{2}k_{\text{eff}}x^2$. So small oscillations of almost anything are harmonic — which is why the oscillator reappears in **waves**, the **quantum harmonic oscillator**, and quantum fields.

### Watch out

Amplitude-independence holds only while the restoring force stays **linear**. Push a real pendulum to large angles and the $\sin\theta\approx\theta$ approximation fails; the period then depends on amplitude and the motion is no longer simple harmonic. Linearity is the hidden assumption.


### Energy in the oscillation

Tracking energy makes the motion vivid. At the extremes of the swing the mass is momentarily at rest — all energy is potential, $\tfrac{1}{2}kA^2$. At the center it moves fastest — all energy is kinetic, $\tfrac{1}{2}mv_{\max}^2$. Since the two must be equal, $v_{\max} = A\sqrt{k/m} = A\omega$. The energy sloshes back and forth at *twice* the oscillation frequency (it peaks twice per cycle), while the total stays fixed — a clean illustration of energy conservation in motion.

### Damping and resonance, the next chapter

Real oscillators lose energy to friction (**damping**), so the amplitude decays. If you also drive the system periodically, something dramatic happens near its natural frequency $\omega$: the amplitude grows large — **resonance**. This is why a pushed swing soars when timed right, why a wine glass shatters at the correct pitch, and why bridges must avoid matching the rhythm of wind or marching feet. Resonance is the practical reason the natural frequency $\omega = \sqrt{k/m}$ is worth knowing for any system.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Wiggle one end of a long rope and the wiggle travels down its length. The strange part: the rope material itself only bobs up and down in place — nothing physically travels the rope except the *pattern*. That moving pattern, carrying energy without carrying matter, is a **wave**.

### Precisely

For a disturbance $y(x,t)$ the **wave equation** is

$$\frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial t^2} = v^2\,\frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial x^2},$$

where $v$ is the propagation speed. The basic relation between speed, frequency $f$ (oscillations per second), and wavelength $\lambda$ (length of one cycle) is

$$v = f\lambda.$$

Solutions include any shape $y = f(x - vt)$ travelling at speed $v$, plus pure sinusoids.

### Worked example

A sound wave in air ($v = 340\ \text{m/s}$) at frequency $f = 170\ \text{Hz}$ has wavelength

$$\lambda = \frac{v}{f} = \frac{340}{170} = 2\ \text{m}.$$

A guitar string of length $L$ fixed at both ends supports standing waves with $\lambda = 2L/n$; the lowest ($n=1$) has $\lambda = 2L$.

### Why it works

The equation is **linear**, so solutions **superpose** — two waves pass through each other and simply add. Where crests align they reinforce (constructive); where crest meets trough they cancel (destructive). On a bounded medium, superposition of waves travelling both ways produces fixed **standing-wave** patterns — the basis of musical pitch.

### Where it connects

It is built from **simple harmonic motion** (each point oscillates) and **calculus**. The very same equation governs **electromagnetic waves** (with $y$ a field and $v=c$). Superposition is the foundation of **wave optics** and Fourier analysis.

### Watch out

A wave transports energy and momentum, **not matter** — the medium stays put on average. And the clean picture assumes $v$ is constant. When $v$ depends on frequency (**dispersion**), different colors or pitches travel at different speeds and a pulse spreads out — the first complication beyond the ideal wave equation.


### Standing waves and music

When a wave is confined — a guitar string fixed at both ends, air in a flute — only wavelengths that "fit" survive, forming **standing waves** with stationary nodes (no motion) and antinodes (maximum motion). A string of length $L$ allows $\lambda_n = 2L/n$, giving a fundamental pitch and a ladder of harmonics above it. The particular mix of harmonics is what makes a violin and a flute playing the same note sound different — the physics of timbre is the physics of standing-wave superposition.

### Fourier: every wave is a sum of sines

Because the wave equation is linear, *any* waveform — a square pulse, a spoken vowel, a drumbeat — can be decomposed into a sum of pure sine waves of different frequencies. This is **Fourier analysis**, and it is one of the most powerful tools in all of physics and engineering. It is why an equalizer can boost the bass, why MP3 compression works, and why analyzing a complicated vibration reduces to studying its simple sinusoidal ingredients one at a time.

The first complication beyond this clean picture is dispersion — when the speed v depends on frequency, so different colors or pitches travel at different speeds and a pulse spreads out.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Electric charge comes in two flavors — positive and negative. Likes repel, opposites attract; you feel it as static cling. The push or pull weakens with the square of distance, exactly like gravity, with one decisive twist: gravity only ever pulls, but electricity can push *and* pull, so electric effects can cancel.

### Precisely

Between two point charges $q_1$ and $q_2$ separated by $r$:

$$\vec F = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{q_1 q_2}{r^2}\,\hat r,$$

where $\varepsilon_0 = 8.85\times10^{-12}\ \text{C}^2/(\text{N·m}^2)$ is the permittivity of free space and charge is measured in coulombs ($\text{C}$). Rather than picture action at a distance, we say each charge creates an **electric field** $\vec E = \vec F/q$ (units $\text{N/C}$) filling space; a second charge then feels $\vec F = q\vec E$.

### Worked example

Two charges $q_1 = q_2 = 1\ \mu\text{C} = 10^{-6}\ \text{C}$ sit $r = 0.1\ \text{m}$ apart. With $k = 1/(4\pi\varepsilon_0) = 8.99\times10^9$:

$$F = k\frac{q_1q_2}{r^2} = (8.99\times10^9)\frac{(10^{-6})^2}{(0.1)^2} = (8.99\times10^9)(10^{-10}) = 0.899\ \text{N},$$

a repulsion since both are positive.

### Why it works

The field $\vec E$ makes electromagnetism **local**: a charge responds to the field at its own location, not directly to distant charges. This bookkeeping becomes essential the moment charges move, because field changes travel at finite speed. The shared $1/r^2$ form with gravity is exactly why both obey a **Gauss law**.

### Where it connects

Coulomb's law builds on **vectors** and parallels **gravitation**. It leads to **Gauss's law**, **electric potential**, and — once charges move — the **magnetic** Lorentz force, since magnetism is electricity seen from a moving frame.

### Watch out

The crucial difference from gravity is the **two signs of charge**: electric fields from different charges can add or cancel, and the force can be attractive or repulsive. Treating electricity as "just like gravity" misses this entirely. Also, Coulomb's law in this simple form is for point charges (or spherical ones, by symmetry).


### Superposition: building real fields

Real situations have many charges, and the electric field obeys **superposition** — the total field is the vector sum of the fields from each charge separately. This is what lets us compute the field of a charged rod, ring, or plate: chop it into tiny charges $dq$, add up their $\vec E$ contributions (an integral), and the linearity of Coulomb's law guarantees the pieces simply add. Superposition is quietly one of the most important properties in all of electromagnetism.

### Comparing the two great inverse-square forces

It is worth dwelling on the gravity comparison. Gravity between two protons is weaker than their electric repulsion by a factor of about $10^{36}$ — electromagnetism utterly dominates at the atomic scale. Yet gravity rules the cosmos, because it has only one sign and never cancels: pile up enough matter and every bit pulls the same way. Electric forces, with two signs, cancel almost perfectly in bulk neutral matter. This sign difference, not strength, is why gravity shapes planets and stars while electricity shapes atoms and chemistry.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Wrap any closed bag around some electric charge and count the field lines poking through the bag's surface. The count depends only on how much charge is sealed *inside* — not on the bag's size or weird shape. Charge inside means net lines coming out; no charge inside means whatever enters also leaves. That simple accounting is Gauss's law.

### Precisely

The **electric flux** through a closed surface (a measure of field lines crossing it) equals the enclosed charge over $\varepsilon_0$:

$$\oint \vec E\cdot d\vec A = \frac{Q_{\text{enc}}}{\varepsilon_0}.$$

The point-by-point (**differential**) form is

$$\nabla\cdot\vec E = \frac{\rho}{\varepsilon_0},$$

where $\rho$ is the local charge density and $\nabla\cdot\vec E$ (divergence) measures how much the field spreads from a point.

### Worked example

Find the field of a point charge $q$. By symmetry $\vec E$ is radial and uniform on a sphere of radius $r$ centered on the charge, so the flux is $E\cdot 4\pi r^2$. Gauss's law gives

$$E\cdot 4\pi r^2 = \frac{q}{\varepsilon_0} \;\Rightarrow\; E = \frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^2}.$$

We recovered Coulomb's law — and got it almost instantly thanks to symmetry.

### Why it works

The trick is that field lines from a point spread over a sphere whose area grows as $r^2$, exactly cancelling the $1/r^2$ fall-off of the field, so the total flux is fixed by the enclosed charge alone. This is a direct consequence of three-dimensional geometry.

### Where it connects

Gauss's law is Coulomb's law restated, but more general — it holds for moving charges too. It is the first of **Maxwell's four equations** and the workhorse for spheres, infinite wires, and charged sheets.

### Watch out

Gauss's law is *always* true, but it only *computes* the field easily when there is enough symmetry to pull $E$ out of the integral. For a lopsided charge blob it still holds, but you can't solve for $E$ from it alone. Also, $Q_{\text{enc}}$ means only the charge *inside* the surface — external charges contribute zero net flux.


### Choosing a Gaussian surface

The skill in using Gauss's law is picking an imaginary closed surface (a "Gaussian surface") that matches the symmetry so the field is constant and either parallel or perpendicular to it everywhere. For a sphere of charge, use a concentric sphere; for an infinite line of charge, a coaxial cylinder; for an infinite sheet, a pillbox straddling it. With the right surface, $\oint\vec E\cdot d\vec A$ collapses to $E$ times an area, and the field falls out in one step — a striking shortcut that would otherwise require a hard integral.

### A surprising result inside conductors

Gauss's law has a profound corollary: inside a conductor in static equilibrium, the electric field is exactly **zero**, and any excess charge sits entirely on the surface. If a field existed inside, it would push the free charges until they rearranged to cancel it. This is why a car or a metal cage shields its interior from external fields (a **Faraday cage**) — lightning can strike the shell and the inside stays safe. The whole effect follows from Gauss's law applied to a surface drawn inside the metal.

For symmetric charge arrangements (a sphere, a long wire, a flat sheet) Gauss's law lets you compute the field almost instantly.

Its very existence is a consequence of the 1/r² geometry of three-dimensional space (field lines from a point spread over a sphere whose area grows as r²).

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

A magnetic field only affects a charge that is *moving* — and it never pushes along the direction of travel. It always shoves sideways, at a right angle. Because the shove is perpetual and perpendicular, the charge curls around in a circle or a corkscrew instead of speeding up. Magnetism, deep down, is just electricity viewed from a moving frame.

### Precisely

The complete force on a charge $q$ from electric field $\vec E$ and magnetic field $\vec B$ (units: tesla, $\text{T}$) moving at velocity $\vec v$ is the **Lorentz force**:

$$\vec F = q\,(\vec E + \vec v\times\vec B).$$

The magnetic part $q\vec v\times\vec B$ uses the cross product, so it is perpendicular to both $\vec v$ and $\vec B$.

### Worked example

A proton ($q = 1.6\times10^{-19}\ \text{C}$) moves at $v = 10^6\ \text{m/s}$ perpendicular to a field $B = 0.5\ \text{T}$. The magnetic force magnitude is

$$F = qvB = (1.6\times10^{-19})(10^6)(0.5) = 8\times10^{-14}\ \text{N},$$

always perpendicular to $\vec v$, so it bends the proton into a circle of radius $r = mv/(qB)$.

### Why it works

Because $\vec F \perp \vec v$, the power delivered is $\vec F\cdot\vec v = 0$ — the magnetic force does **no work** and cannot change the particle's speed, only its direction. A constant-magnitude force forever perpendicular to velocity is precisely the recipe for circular (or helical) motion.

### Where it connects

It builds on **Coulomb** and the **cross product**, and underlies **Faraday's law** and the **Ampère–Maxwell law**. In **special relativity**, $\vec E$ and $\vec B$ are revealed as two faces of one electromagnetic field — what looks magnetic to one observer looks partly electric to another.

### Watch out

The magnetic force **never speeds a particle up or slows it down** — a frequent misconception. It can only redirect. Also mind the right-hand rule and the sign of $q$: a negative charge curls the opposite way. Get the hand or the sign wrong and the whole trajectory inverts.


### The radius of the circle

When a charge enters a uniform field perpendicular to $\vec B$, the magnetic force $qvB$ supplies the centripetal force $mv^2/r$. Equating them gives the orbit radius $r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}$ and the **cyclotron frequency** $f = \dfrac{qB}{2\pi m}$ — remarkably, a frequency independent of the particle's speed. This speed-independence is the operating principle of the cyclotron particle accelerator and of mass spectrometers, which sort ions by the radius of their curved paths.

### Currents are moving charges

A wire carrying current is just a stream of moving charges, so a magnetic field pushes on a current-carrying wire: $\vec F = I\vec L\times\vec B$. This is the force behind every electric motor — a current loop in a field feels a torque that spins it. Conversely, moving a wire through a field generates a current (induction, the next topic). The Lorentz force is thus the single hinge connecting electricity, magnetism, and mechanical motion in every motor and generator on Earth.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Move a magnet near a coil of wire and current flows — with no battery anywhere. A magnet sitting still does nothing; it is the *change* that drives the current. This is how every power plant on Earth generates electricity: spinning magnets past coils.

### Precisely

The **magnetic flux** through a loop is $\Phi_B = \int \vec B\cdot d\vec A$. Faraday's law says the induced **electromotive force** (EMF, a voltage-like push) around the loop equals minus the rate of change of that flux:

$$\oint \vec E\cdot d\vec\ell = -\frac{d\Phi_B}{dt}.$$

The differential form, $\nabla\times\vec E = -\dfrac{\partial\vec B}{\partial t}$, says a changing magnetic field creates a *circulating* (curling) electric field. The minus sign is **Lenz's law**.

### Worked example

A coil of $N = 100$ turns and area $A = 0.01\ \text{m}^2$ sits in a field that changes from $0.2\ \text{T}$ to $0$ in $0.1\ \text{s}$. The EMF is

$$\mathcal{E} = -N\frac{\Delta\Phi_B}{\Delta t} = -100\,\frac{(0 - 0.2)(0.01)}{0.1} = +2\ \text{V}.$$

The sign tells you the induced current opposes the *decrease* in flux.

### Why it works

The minus sign encodes **Lenz's law**: the induced current flows so as to oppose the change that created it. If it reinforced the change instead, you'd get runaway energy from nothing — so Lenz's law is energy conservation in disguise.

### Where it connects

Faraday's law builds on the **magnetic Lorentz force** and **calculus**. It is the first equation showing electric fields born from *changing magnetism* (closed loops, not from charges), and together with the **Ampère–Maxwell law** it makes self-sustaining **electromagnetic waves** possible.

### Watch out

It is the **change** in flux that matters, not the flux itself — a strong but steady field induces nothing. Flux can change three ways: changing $B$, changing the loop's area, or rotating the loop (as in a generator). And never drop the minus sign; it is the whole physical content of Lenz's law.


### Motional EMF: the generator from the other side

There are two ways to picture induction, and they agree. If you *move a conductor* through a steady field, the free charges in it feel the magnetic Lorentz force $q\vec v\times\vec B$, which pushes them along the wire — a "motional EMF." If instead the *field changes* through a stationary loop, Faraday's law says a real circulating electric field appears. A spinning generator uses the first picture; a transformer uses the second. Both are captured by the single law $\mathcal{E} = -d\Phi_B/dt$.

### Transformers and the grid

Faraday's law makes the entire power grid possible. A **transformer** is two coils sharing a changing magnetic flux; the voltage ratio equals the turns ratio, $V_2/V_1 = N_2/N_1$. This lets power be stepped up to hundreds of thousands of volts for low-loss long-distance transmission, then stepped back down for home use. Because it relies on *changing* flux, a transformer works only with alternating current — a deep reason AC, not DC, won the early "war of currents.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

What makes a magnetic field? First, electric current — charges flowing through a wire, known for two centuries. Second, and far more surprising: a *changing electric field*, even in empty space with no wire at all. That second source, added by Maxwell, is the missing piece that makes light possible.

### Precisely

The **Ampère–Maxwell law** in differential form:

$$\nabla\times\vec B = \mu_0\vec J + \mu_0\varepsilon_0\frac{\partial\vec E}{\partial t},$$

where $\vec J$ is the current density, $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \text{T·m/A}$ is the permeability of free space, and the second term $\mu_0\varepsilon_0\,\partial\vec E/\partial t$ is Maxwell's **displacement current** — a changing electric field acting like a current for the purpose of making $\vec B$.

### Worked example (conceptual)

Charge a parallel-plate capacitor through a wire. Real current $\vec J$ flows in the wire and produces a circling $\vec B$ around it. But between the plates there is a *gap* — no charges cross. Yet a magnetic field still encircles that gap. What sources it? The growing electric field between the plates: the displacement-current term supplies exactly the right $\vec B$, with the same magnitude as the wire's current would give, keeping the field continuous.

### Why it works

Ampère's original law alone violated charge conservation wherever current was interrupted (like the capacitor gap). Maxwell's term repairs this: it is precisely what makes the equations consistent with the **continuity equation** $\nabla\cdot\vec J + \partial\rho/\partial t = 0$. It is also the mirror image of Faraday's law — a changing $\vec E$ makes $\vec B$, just as a changing $\vec B$ makes $\vec E$.

### Where it connects

It builds on the **magnetic Lorentz force**, **Gauss's law**, and **Faraday's law**, and completes **Maxwell's equations**. The mutual feedback it creates with Faraday's law is the engine of **electromagnetic waves**.

### Watch out

The displacement current is *not* a flow of charge — nothing physically moves in the capacitor gap. It is a changing field that *acts like* a current for generating $\vec B$. Treating it as literal current flow is a common conceptual error. Its real job is enforcing charge conservation and enabling radiation.


### Symmetry restored

With Maxwell's addition, the two "curl" equations become near-mirror images: a changing magnetic field makes a circulating electric field (Faraday), and a changing electric field makes a circulating magnetic field (Ampère–Maxwell). This symmetry is not just elegant — it is the mechanical reason a disturbance can propagate. Wiggle a charge, and its changing electric field sources a magnetic field, whose change sources an electric field further along, and the pattern marches off at speed $c$. Without the displacement-current term there would be no light.

### Sizing the displacement current

The displacement current is genuinely comparable to ordinary current in the right setting. In a charging capacitor, the displacement current through the gap exactly equals the conduction current in the wires — which is why the magnetic field is continuous as you slide an imaginary loop from around the wire to around the gap. Maxwell did not add a small correction; he added the term that makes the whole theory consistent and complete, and it carries as much "current" as the wire it bridges.

He fixed it by adding the 'displacement current' term μ₀ε₀ ∂E/∂t (μ₀, 'mu-naught', is the magnetic counterpart of ε₀), which says a changing electric field acts like a current for making magnetic fields. With this addition the four Maxwell equations become complete and self-consistent.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Just four rules describe everything about electricity and magnetism: where the fields come from and how they create each other. Put them together and they hand you an unexpected gift — they predict that light exists and travels at one fixed speed, built entirely from electric and magnetic constants.

### Precisely

In differential form:

$$\nabla\cdot\vec E = \rho/\varepsilon_0,\quad \nabla\cdot\vec B = 0,\quad \nabla\times\vec E = -\partial_t\vec B,\quad \nabla\times\vec B = \mu_0\vec J + \mu_0\varepsilon_0\,\partial_t\vec E.$$

In words: (1) charges source $\vec E$ (Gauss); (2) no magnetic monopoles — $\vec B$ lines never start or end; (3) changing $\vec B$ makes curling $\vec E$ (Faraday); (4) currents and changing $\vec E$ make curling $\vec B$ (Ampère–Maxwell).

### Worked example

In empty space ($\rho = 0$, $\vec J = 0$), take the curl of Faraday's law and substitute Ampère–Maxwell. Using $\nabla\times(\nabla\times\vec E) = -\nabla^2\vec E$, one gets

$$\nabla^2\vec E = \mu_0\varepsilon_0\frac{\partial^2\vec E}{\partial t^2},$$

a wave equation with speed

$$c = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(8.85\times10^{-12})}} \approx 3.0\times10^8\ \text{m/s}.$$

That is the measured speed of light — derived from electromagnetism alone.

### Why it works

Faraday's and Ampère–Maxwell's laws couple $\vec E$ and $\vec B$ so each changing field regenerates the other. Eliminating one field leaves a self-contained wave equation; the propagation speed is fixed by $\mu_0$ and $\varepsilon_0$, with no reference to any observer's motion.

### Where it connects

The four equations unify **Gauss's law**, **Faraday's law**, and **Ampère–Maxwell**, and produce **electromagnetic waves**. That $c$ is observer-independent clashed with Galilean velocity addition and forced **special relativity**.

### Watch out

A subtle point: it was *Newtonian mechanics*, not Maxwell's equations, that had to be corrected to satisfy relativity — Maxwell's equations were already Lorentz-invariant. Also, $\nabla\cdot\vec B = 0$ is an experimental fact (no monopole has ever been found), not a derived identity.


### Two equations for sources, two for dynamics

It helps to group the four. The two **divergence** equations describe sources: $\nabla\cdot\vec E = \rho/\varepsilon_0$ says charges make electric fields that spread outward, and $\nabla\cdot\vec B = 0$ says there are no magnetic charges, so magnetic field lines always close on themselves. The two **curl** equations describe dynamics: how each field is stirred into circulation by the other's change. Together with the Lorentz force law (which says how fields push charges), this is the *complete* theory of classical electromagnetism — everything from radio to optics follows.

### A theory ahead of its time

Maxwell assembled these equations in the 1860s, and they already had relativity built in, decades before Einstein. Because they predict one fixed speed $c$ with no preferred frame, they quietly demanded that space and time behave in the Lorentz way. When experiments (Michelson–Morley) failed to find the expected "ether wind," it was mechanics, not Maxwell, that had to bend. The equations are a rare case of mathematics correctly anticipating a revolution in physics.

Together they form a closed, self-contained system. From these four alone you can derive that the fields travel as waves at speed c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀) — and plugging in the measured constants gives exactly the speed of light.
depths.deep: That this speed c comes out of purely electric and magnetic constants — with no mention of any observer's motion — clashed head-on with the older Galilean idea that speeds should add. That contradiction is what pushed Einstein to special relativity. Remarkably, Maxwell's equations were already 'Lorentz-invariant' (they obey relativity's symmetry); it was Newton's mechanics that had to be corrected.
